name: Sara Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, parties or government. This is confidential. What does a usual workday hold?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, and I lead the escalation desk for a contact centre. I finished a two-year college diploma and became one of the agents people call over when a delivery story does not match a bill. The pay is higher than most people in this job receive. I use an approved AI summary tool now and then, after other agents show me it works on that type of chat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes the work worthwhile, and what tires you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding the one missing date that clears up a complaint. I dislike a dashboard that counts a fast reply as a solved case. I live alone and have nine months of expenses saved, so I can challenge a poor shortcut without fearing next month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the reminder tool saves a few clicks, and that is fine. A reminder tool won't settle a customer whose delivery and bill tell different stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel secure here. I'm paid above the usual rate because I lead the escalation desk, and my savings cover nine months of rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay on escalations and keep using the approved tool for short summaries when it gets the details right. Through the first year I'll add the saved minutes to weekly coaching, not cut a person from the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little satisfaction that the human part stays visible. I don't need a bigger promise from the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check before passing a summary along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I test one summary against the customer's original chat and correct it before an agent takes the case. If the tool misses the delivery date, I do not pass the summary along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the separate account for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I live alone and keep the nine-month reserve in a separate account. It is there for a serious gap, not for buying the latest app.

say: I'd accept **small shortcuts** on routine chat summaries once an agent checks the original customer account.
I'd keep **mixed delivery disputes** with an agent.
think: I feel **secure** on the escalation desk with higher pay than most agents here.
My **nine-month reserve** covers a long gap if work changes.
do: Keep leading **escalation calls** through the first year.
Use **approved summaries** only after checking the original chat.
Coach agents with the **saved minutes** each week.
feel: **Calm**, with satisfaction that careful listening still matters.
S0.quote: A reminder tool won't settle a customer whose delivery and bill tell different stories.
fieldNote: She earns **higher pay** for leading difficult escalations.
Her **tool use** follows a check against the source chat.
Her **nine-month reserve** protects her without inviting speculative spending.

steps.text: Keep leading customer escalation calls this year
Check approved AI summaries against original chats

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the first test is whether a customer reaches the right person after the bot answers. If easy chats vanish, our old time target should change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the centre could stop hiring beginners and ask senior agents to handle only tangled cases. My role may be safe for now, but I don't want new agents blamed for a harder queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll use the approved handoff checker after two colleagues have tested it and record where callers repeat themselves. I'll bring those counts to a staff meeting with the two colleagues; if a posted paid quality post opens locally in the first year, I'll compare its wage with mine before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. I have savings and local options, but the entry path for my team could narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your colleagues count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would count repeat explanations, not just minutes saved. I would ask the manager to put a new time target in writing for the harder calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a new role worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would only apply for a job with a clear wage close to my present higher pay. I won't take a title that lowers my monthly income while my rent stays the same.

say: I'd test whether **bot handoffs** reach the right agent before calling the new process a success.
I'd request **new time targets** for harder calls.
think: I worry my **new agents** could be blamed for a harder queue.
do: Use the **proven handoff checker** on repeat calls this month.
Bring **repeat-call counts** with colleagues to the staff meeting.
Apply for a **posted paid quality role** only near my current wage.
feel: **Uneasy** about the team's entry path, while my own income seems safe.
S1.quote: I won't take a title that lowers my monthly income while my rent stays the same.
fieldNote: She waits for **colleague tests** before adopting a new checker.
Her **group evidence** supports a new target for harder calls.
She protects a **higher wage** even with plenty of local options.

steps.text: Use approved handoff checker after colleagues test it
Present repeat-call counts with two colleagues at the staff meeting
Apply for posted paid quality roles only near her present wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell agents that full thinking AI by 2028 could answer our calls, however good our own scripts are. Robots around 2031 are a later problem for hands-on jobs, not a grace period for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my escalation role might vanish, too. Nine months saved buys search time, but local contact centres may all cut the same work, and that frightens me more than a single layoff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll collect anonymised examples where an automated answer made a dispute worse. If my role goes in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for posted paid complaints-review jobs outside call centres and keep my rent covered from savings while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quite sharply. I have a practical buffer, but I cannot make a vacancy appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the agents I lead what I know and what I don't know about staffing. I would ask management for a dated plan in writing before I repeat any reassurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you search beyond call centres?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would search utilities and delivery firms for paid review posts, checking the wage before sending an application. I would apply only if it stays close to my current lead pay. A complaints-review vacancy that pays much less than my current lead job would eat my reserve every month.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** could answer our calls.
I'd explain **2031 robots** give phone agents no extra time.
think: I fear my **escalation role** may vanish even though I handle the difficult customer cases.
I know **nine months saved** cannot create local vacancies.
do: Apply for **posted paid review posts** after a job cut only if wages stay close to my current lead pay.
Use **savings for rent** during an actual search.
feel: **Anxious** about a field-wide cut despite a strong buffer.
S2.quote: A complaints-review vacancy that pays much less than my current lead job would eat my reserve every month.
fieldNote: Her **high skill** does not shelter her from general thinking AI.
She names **outside employers** to avoid relying on nearby centres alone.
Her **wage check** guards against slowly draining savings.

steps.text: Apply for posted paid review jobs after a cut only near current lead pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years is enough to ask employers for actual paid learning time. Call work changes in 2031, while robots doing hands-on work follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become good at reviewing difficult service decisions by then. I would rather learn from real complaint cases than pay for a vague qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask my manager for a paid half-day each month to shadow the complaints-review team. If approved, I'll complete their supervised review module before 2031; in the first year after AGI, I'll apply for a posted paid reviewer vacancy only if its wage covers my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused, with some worry about the junior agents. I can plan a route, but the centre may not create enough posts for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the review team to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the review team to show me cases they changed after a customer appealed. That would tell me what the work really involves before I commit the paid study hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would juniors share the shadowing time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would make sure a junior agent can shadow as well if the manager funds the time. My own route should not be the only one visible on the rota.

say: I'd seek **paid shadowing** before 2031 so I can learn what complaints reviewers actually do.
I'd remind colleagues **2034 robots** arrive after our call work changes.
think: I could build **review skill** through real cases.
I doubt there will be **enough posts** for every junior agent.
do: Shadow **complaints reviewers** only during approved paid time.
Complete the **supervised module** if paid time is granted.
Apply for a **posted paid reviewer job** only if wages cover rent.
feel: **Focused**, with concern for junior colleagues' chances.
S3.quote: I would rather learn from real complaint cases than pay for a vague qualification.
fieldNote: Her **five-year plan** relies on funded time and supervised cases.
She weighs **junior access** alongside her own next role.
Her **rent threshold** remains attached to any vacancy.

steps.text: Complete supervised complaints-review module during approved paid hours
Apply for posted paid reviewer jobs only if wages cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets the centre train people gradually and tell customers what changes. The date for our thinking work is 2036; robots around 2039 belong to a different part of the economy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 27 I can keep a job I do well and test another route over time. Nine months saved means I can reject an offer that does not fit, though I still want proper wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep the escalation shift and ask for one paid review session each quarter. If those sessions are approved, I'll learn the appeal process from actual cases; before and during the first year after 2036, I'll check posted paid reviewer roles and move only if the wage covers my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and interested. Ten years lets me learn without turning my savings into a training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a record of appeals I helped solve, without names or account numbers. A future interviewer could see how I reached an answer, not just how many calls I closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell new agents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell new agents that they can learn during paid shifts. Checking a bot's answer is a real skill when it protects a customer. They should ask for that time on the rota.

say: I'd favour **gradual training** through the decade, with paid time to practise on real appeals.
I'd separate **2036 call work** from 2039 robots.
think: I can **test another route** while still earning well.
I can refuse a **poor wage offer** with nine months saved.
do: Learn the **appeal process** in approved paid quarterly sessions.
Move to a **posted paid reviewer role** only if wages cover rent.
feel: **Calm and interested** because learning can fit around paid work.
S4.quote: Checking a bot's answer is a real skill when it protects a customer.
fieldNote: She treats the **long window** as time to test, not resign.
Her **quarterly sessions** require approved paid hours.
Her **nine-month reserve** lets her reject wages below her rent needs.

steps.text: Keep leading the customer escalation shift this year
Learn appeals during approved paid quarterly review sessions
Move to posted paid reviewer job only if wages cover rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My own job could shrink before I have tested a move, and nearby centres might cut at once. A dated staffing plan, paid shadowing and real reviewer vacancies would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask if the customer can still appeal a bot's answer. A quick answer that cannot be challenged is not a settled case. Someone needs to own the correction.

headlineQuote: A quick answer that cannot be challenged is not a settled case.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old lead** on a contact-centre escalation desk, with a two-year diploma and strong complaint skills.
She earns **higher pay**, lives alone and has nine months saved; many similar centres are nearby.
She uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues test it and checks summaries against customer records.
The **2028 deadline** worries her most; longer timelines support paid shadowing and applications for posted review roles.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may cut her role while nearby centres make similar reductions.
whatWouldHelp: A dated **staffing plan** would show when work changes.
**Paid shadowing** and real reviewer vacancies would give her a route to test.
